# Kaṇhadīpāyanajātaka (Ja 444)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Black Dīpāyana

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kaṇhadīpāyanajātaka* (Ja 444) is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. According to its opening narrative framework (*nidāna*), the Buddha related the tale at Jetavana concerning a discontented or backsliding monk (*ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu*), with reference made to the story of the *Kusajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. In the traditional identification (*samodhāna*) at the conclusion, the characters of the past are matched to disciples of the present: the ascetic Āṇimaṇḍavya was Sāriputta, the wife was Visākhā, the son was Rāhula, and the seer Kaṇhadīpāyana was the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1887].

The central tale concerns the sage Kaṇhadīpāyana and his ascetic friend Maṇḍavya [Geiger 1953; Hazra 1994]. According to the commentary, the Bodhisatta was originally called Dīpāyana; he gained the name *Kaṇhadīpāyana* (*kaṇha* meaning "black") after keeping vigil beside Maṇḍavya while the latter was impaled on a stake, his body stained black by Maṇḍavya's dripping blood [Boriharnwanaket; Geiger 1953]. When Maṇḍavya's son is bitten by a venomous snake, Kaṇhadīpāyana saves the boy through an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) [Hazra 1994]. His solemn declaration of truth revealed that while he had lived the ascetic life (*brahmacariya*) dissatisfied for over fifty years—restrained only by conscience and fear of blame—he had dwelt in it with authentic confidence and joy for merely seven days [SuttaCentral; Boriharnwanaket]. Owing to this declaration, the narrative is featured in the *Cariyāpiṭaka* (Cp 31) to illustrate the Bodhisatta's perfection of truthfulness (*saccapāramī*) [Hazra 1994; Boriharnwanaket]. Scholars have also noted the text's ethical perspectives on family relations and desire [Lewis and Tuladhar 2000].

DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse between Ja 444 and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (26 matches) and *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* (8 matches), as well as four shared passages with the *Kaṇhadīpāyanacariya* (Cp 31, particularly §1.1–1.7 ↔ Cp 31 §11.1–12.3) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects computational alignments with the Tibetan *Bodhisattvacaryāvatāratātparyapañjikāviśeṣadyotanī* (D3880) and two sections of the Chinese *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100) [DharmaNexus].
